utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, would you like to call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Can we have the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, Counsel. For the Prosecution, Daryl Mundis, Ekkehard Withopf, and Ruth Karper, the case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now the appearances for the Defence, who are complete this morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of General Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, lead counsel; Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel; and Alexis Demirdjian, legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And the other Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Chamber bids good morning to everyone. The witness in the first place, who is here present, the representatives of the Prosecution, the Defence lawyers, and all the staff of this courtroom. Before beginning or, rather, continuing the cross-examination of the witness, two small points: The first has to do with the problem that we had regarding the objections made by one or the other party during the production of a document to be tendered into evidence. The rule is an objection is made; the other party responds. There may be a replica, and then a new response, and we stop there. Otherwise, this would go on for hours. The Chamber deliberated on this matter yesterday and finds that when an objection is made, a legal explanation should be given for that objection. Then the other party should be given a chance to respond. And then if the party making the objection feels it is necessary to add something, it does so. And then finally, the floor is given to the other party, and thereby the debate is closed. Otherwise, this debate can go on endlessly. That is the practice at hearings. I just wanted to remind us of that. Also, there was the production of a document entitled "Milinfosum." And the Prosecution provided a translation in French for which the Chamber wishes to thank the Prosecution, because it makes it easier to compare the three different versions. Those are the points I wish to make. Can we continue with the cross-examination now. I turn to Defence counsel, and I give them the floor for the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Madam Judge. Good morning, Your Honour. Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Bower.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Major Bower, we have had the opportunity of meeting this week, so you already know me. But for the record, I'd just like to say my name is Stephane Bourgon, and this morning I am accompanied with my colleague, Mrs. Residovic and my colleague Mr. Alexis Demirdjian and that together we represent General Hadzihasanovic. I take this opportunity, Major Bower, for thanking you for taking the time to meet with us this week, which I believe should help us to move more quickly this morning. I would also like to confirm before I begin with my questions that you have testified both in the Blaskic case and in the Kordic case and that on both occasions you were called by the Prosecution. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. It was for the Prosecution in both cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would I be right in saying that because of the two times that you testified before the International Tribunal and the proceedings which took place before you coming here this week, that you had a number of opportunities to discuss your experience in Bosnia with representatives from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: With investigators from the Prosecution that you met on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I have discussed my experiences in Bosnia with a number of investigation teams and obviously with a number of Prosecution counsels relating to those cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And before coming here this week, am I right in saying that the last time you met with investigators from the Prosecution was in 2001, at which time you provided the investigators with a statement that you signed to acknowledge that it was to the best of your knowledge true?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Also before I begin, I'd just like to - out of curiosity -- because yesterday you mentioned that you had served as a military officer in Canada. And as you know, I was a major, an infantry officer also in Canada. So where in Canada did you serve?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Medicine Hat at the British army training unit, Suffield.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In Suffield?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: What year was that?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, you also mentioned that you were a member -- now, that's just at the point you arrived in Bosnia -- that you were a member of the support weapons company. What exactly did you do in the support weapons company?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the anti-tank platoon commander in the support weapons company of the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that at that time you were not involved with the mortars platoon or with any type of indirect fire support?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not directly related to the mortar platoon or anything to do with them at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Major. Now, you mentioned yesterday that the days that you were in Bosnia were from approximately the 24th of April, 1993 until the 6th or the 7th of November; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: From -- from what I can recall, those were the approximate dates, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you acknowledge that the mission or the aim of the UNPROFOR mission was humanitarian in principle.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was certainly how it was described to us. The mission statement we were given was very much related to UNHCR and the provision of humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And yourself, Major Bower, as a member of the United Kingdom Army, the name -- the code name used for the operation in your particular case was Operation Grapple II; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the -- the term given for our deployment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And Operation Grapple I would have been the Cheshire Regiment, which preceded you?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's right. The number of the Grapple depicted the number of the battalions going in.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And with respect to the chain of command for an officer of the British Army, you would respond first to your commanding officer of your unit, which responded to the British chain of command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is this during the deployment or in general?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: During the deployment.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depending on which officer we mean. If it was an officer within a rifle company, he would report to his company commander, who would then report to the battalion commander. As a liaison officer, I reported directly to the battalion commander, who -- he had a -- he had two chains of command, a UN chain of command and a British chain of command. And the British --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Major, do you acknowledge that there is a difference between operational control and operational command?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is. But again, with the national support element based in Split, we still had a British brigadier, who still had influence over what we did within the mandate given to us by the British government.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So can it be said, Major Bower, that the -- as part of the UNPROFOR mission you were under operational control of the United Nations and the United Nations BH command, located in Kiseljak, but nevertheless you remained under operational command of the British Army through the national support element located in Split? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, with respect to disciplinary matters within your unit, would I be correct in saying that any disciplinary issues arising during your tour in Bosnia would be dealt with through the operational command, which would be completely the United Kingdom chain of command?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are disciplinary issues of British soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Of British soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they would be dealt with internationally by the battalion commander under his powers of judicial authority given to him. If he was unable to deal with them, they would go to the -- the next British senior officer, which would be based in Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, for yourself and for other British soldiers, if we -- the law in force or basically the applicable law with respect to military duties was the law of the UK; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, would I be right in saying that during your tour in Bosnia the -- the applicable law in Bosnia and Herzegovina was not something that you paid much attention to because you knew what law applied to you?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We'd been given certain conditions with -- within which we had to operate, which were briefed to us. I can't honestly say whether they were specifically created for our deployment or by who, but we were certainly given some parameters with which to operate within -- I'm unaware and I don't know of any local laws, so I wouldn't be able to compare, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Major Bower. Now, would I be right in saying that during that tour in Bosnia you were not particularly aware of the law which applied to the parties of the conflict? For example, to the HVO or the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Local law, no. Very -- very little information was given, if any at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And for yourself, Major Bower, in fact the legal status of the HVO or of the ABiH, pursuant to the law of the Republic of Bosnia in force at the time, is not something that you paid particular attention to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution would appreciate if my learned friend from the Defence side would explain to the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution the relevance of these questions and the line of questioning he's currently pursuing with that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Bourgon. In the question that you formulated, could you indicate the relevance of your question so that we can grasp the meaning. Otherwise, the Prosecution and the Chamber may get the impression that you are departing from the subject. Could you indicate where you're heading so that we can all understand better. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if my learned friend would allow me to put my next question, everything will be quite clear. But I can add at this stage already that this witness held a position in G-5, which was a liaison position with the civilian authorities, and that is why these questions are being put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] -- And concerning the -- were you aware during your time in Bosnia of the legal relationship which existed between the ABiH and the civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, unaware of any relationship.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, Major Bower, I'll move on to another line of questioning with respect to the preparations leading to your deployment in Bosnia and Herzegovina. You mentioned yesterday that you were given very general information on the background and only a very broad overview of the current situation on the ground. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The broad overview we were given on arrival in Split. The -- the detail was given to us on our ten-day handover between the Grapple I battalion, and that was on a one-to-one basis with the individuals with whom we took over from.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you mentioned yesterday that -- so -- that you had little specific information before deploying, because then you concentrated on deployment training. So such, for example, rules of engagement and self-defence scenarios, stuff like that. But then when you arrived, that's when they gave you in Split more detailed information.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. It sort of very much started with general overviews, general scenarios, the locations and the -- the overall situation, political as well, what we call the big picture. And it only went to specific on arrival, actually, in the Lasva Valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Major. But you knew from the information you were given that the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina had gained its independence in 1992 and that it had been admitted as a member of the United Nations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember we were given a briefing as to the overall situation. I can't recall exactly what we were briefed, but that generally fits with the very brief view we were given as the overall start of the -- those troubles which were -- which forced us in in Grapple II.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did you know that the -- the day that the Bosnia and Herzegovina was recognised as a state, that on the same day it was attacked by the Yugoslavia -- Yugoslavian Army and the Serb forces? Was that part of the information you were given?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I honestly can't remember at this moment in time. I've seen programmes since, and so I can't recall whether it -- my memory is due to the programmes I've seen or the briefing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, when you arrived in Split, the kind of information that you were -- would have been provided with would include details on the warring factions, personalities involved, location of units, capabilities, and, of course, weapons system.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, in fact, you probably were provided with some kind of org charts, the military language, or organigrammes reflecting the armies involved in the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in Split. We were -- it was still very much regional as to what ethnic breakdown was in what specific territory, and very much it was how the aid agencies were operating, what major routes were supplied, and the overall UNPROFOR mission and how the British Battalion fitted into that mission. What you're referring to is much more given on arrival in Vitez, when we took over from the Cheshire Regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But -- and upon arriving in Vitez with the regiment, were you ever given org charts?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not organisation charts as you or I may recall of it. A wire diagram, a flowchart. It was very much sort of the verbal briefings and a map was used with the -- graphic symbols to depict which units were in which geographic area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, by the time you deployed in Bosnia, Major Bower, you had already -- you were already an experienced military officer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd been on several deployments. You'd have to ask my commanding officer whether he felt I was experienced or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But if we compare with today -- of course, today you are an instructor at the infantry school, and you've got more than 20 years in the military. So of course we can't compare your detailed knowledge of today with what you had then.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it would be safe to say that I had more experience operationally than my peer group, due to my deployment in the Gulf War and several years in Northern Ireland.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, in -- as far as operational experience, which is exactly what I wanted to ask you, this was -- you had been deployed before in Ireland, so you had operational experience. However, am I correct in saying that this was the first time you were deployed into a war where the parties involved were foreign, where territory was new, where the locals did not speak your language, and where you knew not too much about the parties to the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's a -- a safe summary. It was certainly totally different from anything we'd experienced before, because we weren't involved, actually, in the campaign. We were sort of very much, you know, in -- in the middle or almost at points observers to what was going on, rather than participants within. So it was a peculiar and I think it was probably the first time that any of us, including the commanding officer, had been in that kind of situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when you arrived, you were assigned by Lieutenant Colonel Duncan, who was your commander, as the G-5 liaison officer. That's correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I was assigned about two months before deployment. When the roles were given out as to the breakdown of how the officers were going to be employed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, just for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, maybe we could confirm where the term "G-5" comes from, in terms of where do we use G-1, G-2, G-3, G-4, and G-5, and what do these terms mean in the military con text?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military use the terms G-1 through to G-9. It basically identifies G-1, for example, as discipline, G-2 is intelligence, G-3, operations, G-4 is administration, G-5 is now humanitarian liaison, local liaison, and it goes all the way through to -- to G-9. It is just a -- a number and a letter given to denote groupings within staff work and staff headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Would I be correct, Major, in saying that these numbers, from G-1 to G-5, are numbers that are used in many armies in the world and that it's common language amongst a officer to use these terms?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a NATO terminology which is used throughout -- throughout NATO. It may change from G-1 to J- 1, but other than that the number remain the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And Major Bower, the "G-5" stands for cimic [phoen], or civilian military cooperation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it stands for now, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in your capacity as the BritBat G- 5, the focus of your work was humanitarian issues, and that included the handling of the sick and the wounded, as well as all liaison work with organisations such as ICRC, UNHCR, and other NGOs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't specifically get involved with the UNHCR, other than on a case-by-case basis, as they had their own specific liaison officer dedicated to them. But other than that, yes to everything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, Major Bower, that due to the nature of your work if someone within the British Battalion saw the awful consequences of an armed conflict within BritBat it would be the G-5 and it would be you?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I could say that I -- I saw my fair share of the -- the humanitarian impact or the impact to the -- the civil communities as a result of the -- the war which was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in your capacity as G-5, if I recall correctly from yesterday, your area of responsibility went from Zenica to Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on a -- on an east-west line, that's -- that's fair. And then it would sort of be maybe 20 miles either side of that main road.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: From north to south?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: From north to south.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And initially you mentioned that you dealt with doctors and aid agency. But then as the tour progressed, you also had to deal with military commanders and the object of these meetings was to obtain their cooperation for humanitarian activities.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Again, it was a case-by-case, rather than a routine liaison with the -- the military command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And with respect to the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, you dealt most of the time with Colonel Merdan, and you once had to deal directly with General Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. It was Colonel Merdan, and only once from what I can recollect with the general.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And based on what you said to the Trial Chamber yesterday, the -- commenting upon your commander, Lieutenant Colonel Duncan, the relationship between the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and British Battalion was very good and highly professional; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. From -- from what I can recall, his -- his working relationship with the 3 Corps headquarters was cordial.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please make a pause between questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... on hide and seek games with the command of 3rd Corps. Thank you for the information. I'm sorry for the interpreters. I will take a pause between questions.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, could you repeat the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: We speak the same language, so sometimes it's difficult for interpreters. I apologise. So my question was that -- we were speaking about the relationship between the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and 3rd Corps leadership with BritBat, and you mentioned that Lieutenant Colonel Duncan said it was highly professional and that it was also very good. Now, my question was: Did Lieutenant Colonel Duncan ever alluded to or mention any hide-and-seek games with the 3rd Corps leadership that they would be hiding things from him?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I can't recall. Certainly the trade "hide and seek," I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, most of the time you yourself, Major Bower, were granted freedom of movement and the cooperation you received from the 3rd Corps, at least until September, when there might have been a change in the pace of the conflict and to the military advantage that the cooperation you obtained from 3rd Corps was very good. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say on the whole the cooperation was very -- there may be one or two occasions throughout the tour where I may have hindrance getting through. But as a general, yes, I would say that the relationship and the movement that I had was -- in the first two-thirds of the tour was better than it was in the last third.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And until then, Major, you are in the position to acknowledge that the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was in a very difficult position, that they both needed and appreciated the assistance and cooperation, and that for that reason their cooperation was probably better than what you could obtain from the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My -- my time was very much dependent on who was being more effective as a -- as a fighting force and creating more casualties. So I was very much dealing with the resultant clashes. So the HVO were very much in the ascendancy for the first two-thirds, from my perspective, because I was very much dealing with the vast majority of Bosnian Muslim civilians. And as a result, I think just naturally people wanted to help people of their own ethnic grouping. So yes, I had, you know, cooperation when -- when I needed it. There were times when it -- it didn't happen, but that was infrequent, rather than frequent.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, Major Bower, you -- when you testified in the Blaskic and the Kordic cases, you made reference to a number of incidents involving the HVO and the HVO not providing you with cooperation. Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There -- there were occasions when the HVO were -- were a deliberate hindrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, Major Bower, even when the military advantage shifted later in the tour the HVO nevertheless remained not cooperative in many respects with respect to granting you the same type of freedom of movement that you were obtaining from the 3rd Corps; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the last eight weeks, when it -- the balance of fortune shifted, the HVO certainly continued to -- to be unpredictable as to whether they would help or not, but there were times when we didn't get the assistance from 3rd Corps as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, Major Bower, one thing that you did practice during your tour as G-5 is certainly shuttle diplomacy. And if your own words, it was a very frustrating experience. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was frustrated because it was time-consuming, and the original request was often lost in the resultant time and effort resolving add-on linkages.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And even though, Major Bower, you mentioned to me that the British forces were at their beginning with respect to G-5 type of work, you yourself saw or came to realise the importance of your job as G-5.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, I -- I certainly became aware of the impact that I could have. But I was a small team of eight with a battalion of 600 trying to operate as best we could with the resources we had. But it certainly -- it was an addition to the aid agencies who were in the area who either couldn't or wouldn't deal with the -- the situation because of their individual mandates as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, Major Bower, you -- you said earlier that you did see a lot of suffering. And would I be right in saying that still today, when you look back at your tour as G-5, it was something that was a very difficult experience and very often you cannot understand all the misery you witnessed?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that would -- that would sum it up. I mean, I was only there for six months. I didn't live through it. But certainly it was something which -- I certainly still can't understand some of the -- the actions that were taking place during my six months there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And this was, Major Bower, a very emotional job because you dealt mostly with civilians, and there were days, as you said, when you were so disgusted and felt so bad that you did not even attend the 6.00 meeting.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall not attending. It was a compulsory attendance. There would be days when I would be so frustrated that we had just not achieved anything, that we just didn't go out in the afternoon. We had achieved whatever we could, and inevitably failed or things had been cancelled, and so we would cancel the rest of the day. But the 18 hour groups were -- 1800 hour groups were compulsory.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And this brings me to the issue, Major Bower, of the milinfosum, the preparation of which you spoke about yesterday. Am I right in saying that the name given to this document, i.e. military information summary, is based on the fact that UNPROFOR units were not supposed to gather intelligence because this was a Chapter 6 humanitarian mission? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I -- I don't know what the chapter 6 humanitarian mission is, so I -- I can't -- all I can recall is that we were specifically informed that military intelligence was not why we were there, because we weren't involved actively within the campaign. We were very much in the observance role. But we had to capture data of some sort to assist to understand what we were in. And I think that's the reason -- one of the reasons why "information" was the term used and we were specifically told that the term "intelligence" is not to be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: For the benefit of the Trial Chamber, to try and make an illustration, would you agree with me, Major Bower, that if your battalion had been at war the gathering of intelligence would have been much more important and proactive and that additional means, such as human intelligence, electronic devices, satellite imagery and radio intercepts, to name just a few, would have been used?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's fair to say. But I think there would have been more assets within the battalion applied to it. There was one officer and one NCO who were an information cell. Whereas in a battalion in operations of war a lot more would be getting intelligence from all our neighbouring units and our high headquarters, which obviously we were getting very little information at all. It was very much us within our small area as to what we had seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And major Bower, would you agree with me as the use of additional means such as the ones I've mentioned and electronic devices would have allowed you, your battalion - of course, it was a wartime situation or even in this mission - to determine where attacks were to take place, when they were to take place, and by which units coming from which area? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think with the -- the asset which is were available today, if we'd have had them 11 years ago, I think perhaps we'd have been able to track troop movement, depending on which asset, to be able to say which unit they come from would be dependent on the assets which we have. And again, based on intelligence. So whether we could say it is a specific unit or not, I -- I don't know whether we could have done that. We probably may be able to do it now, but I -- it's difficult to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, the reason, Major Bower, why such means were not used is probably because, one, maybe they were not available, or, two, they weren't required for your purpose. And as you said, it wasn't permitted for that type of operation. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I'm aware, it was never discussed. Certainly, you know, the gathering of intelligence that I can recall was just not an option. It wasn't something which was available to us if we'd asked for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, Major Bower, again for -- to allow the Trial Chamber to have a good understanding of this information function, would you agree with me based on your knowledge and experience that in a war situation the movement of troops usually take place at night?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It -- it really does depend on the terrain, the forces you're using, and, you know, the operation you're going to conduct, and what assets the enemy has which you've identified which could detect you. So yes, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sorry. I'm sorry. Let me be more precise. Final combat preparations, final resupply before an attack, and the fact that an attack is usually launched at least one hour before first light is common knowledge amongst all soldiers. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that that's a doctrine which has been adhered to, but it certainly isn't current at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the idea of launching an attack at least one hour before first light is to achieve total surprise and to profit from maximum confusion.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That certainly is one of the benefits of -- of launching an attack at that time of day. But because now everyone expects it at that time, it's almost lost its -- its surprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would you agree with me, Major, that in obtaining that type of information, in terms of the movement of troops, combat preparations, resupply operations, that would allow someone to know where an attack is going to take place, when and which units would attack and in what numbers?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly the -- the tracking of -- of troops and certainly key assets is -- is the vital thing, not just bodies moving. It's more the -- the assets and the formations which are -- are being moved around the battlefield can lead to an indication of where something is going to happen, either a main effort or supporting effort. So certainly battle tracking is an important information-gathering tool to now allow analysis of future operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in your situation with the UNPROFOR, Major Bower, considering that you did not gather intelligence and that you only worked during daylight, this type of information was therefore not available to you; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say it wasn't available. I mean, things moved quite slowly. It wasn't the high-speed manoeuvre warfare which -- which I am used to. It took time to -- to move assets around. But I would say that there were still occasions to track that there was movement going on, but it took a lot longer to build a picture, rather than necessarily today with high-value intelligence-gathering assets we may get a much clearer picture in a much shorter time frame. I would say it was very much elongated and prolonged. Or it may be the fact it was after the event that we identified what those movements were pointing towards. It wasn't always a clear-cut picture that may be implied by CNN today.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the type of information which was obtained by liaison officers, either by personal visual information or by speaking to various locals, can you confirm that your headquarters, located in Vitez, was in territory controlled by the HVO? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that for the -- up until September we were in HVO-controlled territory. But ABiH held the -- the high-ground feature right next to -- adjacent to the camp because they used to shoot at each other and we were in the middle. So we were in HVO territory, but we were pretty much on -- or in between the two front lines. But after a -- an offence by HVO in September, we were then totally an HVO-held area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, referring to your testimony in the Blaskic and Kordic cases, as well as on your direct knowledge, would it be fair to say that the HVO used propaganda as a very effective weapon?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was -- is that propaganda directed at UNPROFOR or is it --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. Propaganda general -- especially with its own population.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there was -- it was safe to say that they certainly gave the impression to the civilians who I dealt with that they were either doing a lot better than they really were and that the situation was a lot better than it really was. I -- I can't really comment as to what other type of propaganda was given, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'd like to give you maybe, Major Bower, a few examples that you may be aware of, again based on your prior testimony and your knowledge. Can you confirm that HVO media reported that the Guca Gora monastery had been set in flames and that upon verification it was determined that not only the monastery had not been set in flames but that Bandol, a Muslim village, had been burned to the ground? Are you aware of this fact?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall any specific HVO references to it. I know that there was a lot of -- exaggerations, a lot of rumour was flying around as to -- after various offences, who had done what to whom and atrocities that are being committed and -- which caused us to try and investigate and verify. But I can say yes, I mean the church in Guca Gora wasn't -- wasn't destroyed. But -- and I know that Bandol was, having been there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you confirm, Major Bower, just with respect to the propaganda issue, that issues such as the following were reported and ultimately found to be untrue: Things like the killing of the priest and the nuns in Brajkovici?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I recall that there was a rumour going round which was prevalent during the summer that -- and I can't remember which village it was from, but I -- I do recall there was a -- accusations going that a priest and two nuns had been crucified on a church door or something like that, which was being spread around, round the HVO area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that ultimately it was proven to be untrue?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I can recall now -- I've not found anything which would confirm that, and I can't recall being told that it was a confirmed atrocity of any sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what about propaganda from HVO media with respect to the hanging of Croats in front of the church in Zenica? Did you hear such allegations?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I -- I don't recall -- I don't recall that -- that incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you recall any propaganda from the HVO with respect to the arrest of 12.000 Croats in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only recall that there was, again, rumours flying that the -- the Croats within Zenica were being contained within a small area and that they were not being treated fairly. You know, they weren't being allowed to leave if they wanted to. But it just seemed to be sort of a -- a general paranoia, if you like, of when you had enclaves within enclaves. There was very much a -- a hostage/siege mentality because there was the Bosnian Muslim area of Stari Vitez within the Croat area of Vitez, which was in a sort of larger pocket of ABiH. And so it went on. And I think it was very much a -- just a general paranoia of what was happening to their friends, relatives, who they'd lost contact with. There was no means for them to communicate. And so rumours were rife around the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, Major, is that fair to say that such propaganda around the area is likely to influence the population and directly reduce the reliability of information you can obtain from such people?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that certainly the information which we were given we couldn't take at face value. It depended on the source, who was giving it to you, and the -- the stress that that person was -- was under and the situation, the personal situation that individual would be in. If that person was in -- either had wounded sort of friends, relatives they wanted to get out, then they were liable to exaggerate the wounds, the whatever, to get your assistance. So there was -- exaggeration was certainly something we had to be aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, Major Bower, on the military side, in terms of information, can you confirm that the creation of the 8th Muslim Brigade was confirmed in a milinfosum and it was later determined that there was never any such unit called 8 Muslim Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I can't recall at all any reference to -- to an 8 Muslim Brigade. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: No problem. If you -- there's something you don't know, absolutely. No problem. Can you confirm, Major Bower, with respect to the milinfosum -- now, you said a couple of things yesterday in response to questions from the Prosecution. You said, for example, that it was not a record of the 6.00 hour group but, rather, it was a summary of what had been seen that day in that it was a summary of one-to-one opinion or views?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'd say that that's a fair statement, because the -- the 1800 hours' meeting discussed all sorts of administration and purely British Battalion issues which were irrelevant really to any other unit. So that's why it wasn't a -- a word-by-word record of that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you also mentioned yesterday that those views -- there was views expressed at this meeting and ultimately sometimes taken into the milinfosum would be difficult to confirm, either a second, third, or fourth time. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The -- the gathering of this -- this information was by an individual, normally a patrol commander or a liaison officer. So it was very much that individual with his interpreter, what he had seen, or what he had learned from discussion with whoever he'd been conversing with. So it was very much a one-to-one, and you would only get a second source of agreement on it if by chance -- or somebody was specifically told to go to another area to try and confirm or deny something.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Moving on to another topic, Major Bower. You mentioned that you had contacts with brigades from the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And you mentioned specifically the 325 Brigade, because you had contacts with them. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You also mentioned, if I'm correct, that you were given information to the effect that 7 Brigade was a manoeuvre unit which came to be used as a combat indicator. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say after a period of time - and I think it was some time; it wasn't an initial decision that was either given to us. It was something which -- a conclusion which we came to after a period of time, having seen how the situation started to -- to appear and how the overall campaign was -- was being conducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you explained that a combat indicator is when a certain unit is found at a certain place you can anticipate that an attack will take place because this has happened before on more than one occasion. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Either a unit or a high-value asset, a piece of equipment which is unusual in that particular area, something of that nature which -- but it has to be a pattern which builds up. It can't just be taken once and therefore assumed that is a pattern. A pattern has to be something which we've seen at least more than once. And normally it's a chain of events rather than just one specific event.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You also mentioned, Major Bower, that you were given information about the presence of mercenaries in Central Bosnia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. We were briefed in Split specifically about the presence of mercenaries in the whole Bosnia and Herzegovina area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you were also given information at some point that within 7 Brigade there was an element which strictly adhered to the principles of Islam.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall if it was put quite in those terms, but certainly we were informed that there were -- there was an element. It wasn't a large element. It was maybe 100, 150 people maximum. I don't think anybody actually got a -- an exact number of mercenaries who were more adherent to the Islamic codes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And Mayor Bower, you also said that you were given some information which you obtained at some point that the Mujahedin in Central Bosnia functioned as a formed unit and not in small individual groups; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can't remember whether that was information given to us or whether that was a conclusion which we drew to, but certainly it's -- it's what I feel as how that particular mercenary element were fought or was used.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you yourself, Major Bower, you met the Mujahedin for the first time working as some kind of -- what appeared to be a unit with weapons on the 13th of June in Guca Gora; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I'm not sure of the exact date. June potentially, yes -- I really -- I'm afraid I can't recall the exact date. But certainly the first time I came across the Mujahedin was that time in Guca Gora with Major Vaughan Kent-Payne.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, we will come back to this event later on. From now what I would simply like to review with you is what you said about the -- what are the characteristics of a Mujahedin. And you mentioned yesterday that they could be recognised by their features and that this would include facial hair and the fact that they had beards, the fact that their attitude towards UNPROFOR, which was negative; by the style of their dress; by the fact that people were and should be scared of them; that they were unpredictable; that they had more weapons, knives, rocket -- RPGs; and that they were arrogant and that you could only meet them by accident because you did not know their location. All of these things, would that be a fair summary of what you said, in terms of the characteristics of the Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say so, and the fact that they -- they weren't European in appearance as well. Certainly the majority which we saw were Middle Eastern in appearance, rather than European in appearance.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And with respect to uniforms, you mentioned that many of them had combat jackets but they also had baggy trousers and it was nevertheless a mix of clothing, military and other. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly with the ones which I saw on that day, that's -- that's accurate, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say that the Mujahedin had the reputation for being ready to die for Islam, contrary to normal soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I wouldn't say that that was a -- a predominant sort of feature with us at the time. This was really our first encounter with that particular element. It wasn't something which I would say was -- was predominant on that aspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you mentioned that they were not the kind of troops which would not -- which would be used to man checkpoints. Now, my question is: You never met any Mujahedin at the numerous checkpoints that you had to cross?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that correct --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall meeting any -- what I would term "Mujahedin" that -- there were an element of people who, if I could say, were pretending to be Mujahedin or would -- we called them pseudo- or plastic Mujahedin. They would have the badges on, but really weren't involved. You would see one or two of them at a checkpoint but I wouldn't -- we wouldn't class them as that Mujahedin mercenary element.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Cow con -- can you confirm some of the following facts with respect to -- they had to deal with the characteristics that we discovered of Mujahedin. The first one is the location of units of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina is a thing that was well known within your battalion. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I can recall, the military liaison officers who dealt specifically with military headquarters knew very good detail what elements were within that specific area. I'm afraid I can't remember, because I wasn't really involved in that aspect, so I'm afraid I couldn't answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, the -- most of the soldiers from the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, it wasn't a common thing to wear a beard; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I can recall, no, it wasn't a -- a common thing. Certainly the beards which we saw with the Mujahedin were, if I can phrase it, a very full beard, rather than sort of a trimmed beard like what you're wearing yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You are aware, Major Bower, that the weapons situation within the ABiH was critical and in fact that they were so short of weapons that they had about one weapon for each three men? Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall the exact numbers, but certainly it would be -- it would be fair to say that they weren't -- that weapons were not in abundance and there were sort of -- there would be times you would find checkpoints where not everybody had a weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if we look at ABiH soldiers. In general, from your experience of meeting with these soldiers, they had a good attitude towards the UN and the relationship between the UN and BritBat was very good.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: From my experience, you built up relationships with the terrain-holding soldiers because you saw them on a regular basis and they got to know you. But again, dependent on -- or if I could say, it depended on what had happened that day. If they had suffered or they knew that Bosnian Muslim civilians were suffering, then obviously they would get frustrated and ultimately they would take it out on the only people which they could, which would be us. So in hindsight, which is a wonderful thing, as we know, I would -- I can now sympathise with how they reacted. But at the time I couldn't. I was more focussed on what I was trying to do. But certainly over a period of time with individuals at certain areas we built up good relations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And Major Bower, the local population were not scared to hang around close to checkpoints where the normal ABiH soldiers would be; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- the majority of checkpoints which I went there -- through, the only one which I can recall was the Cajdras checkpoint, which yes, there was -- there was a civilian population around it. But as you got closer to the front line and pretty much a front-line checkpoint, I would say there were less civilians there and, and quite understandable.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned something about the unpredictable character of the Mujahedin, and you gave an example of the Mujahedin which -- whom you met in Guca Gora who refused to speak to your female interpreter. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it -- that's correct. Initially when we arrived, they refused to speak to us, through our female interpreter. But obviously after the incident with the firearm, they then did. But then again, as we were moving to the village to look for this alleged grave site, there were further Mujahedin who refused to speak to us and we had to sort of do a three-way conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, the fact that a Mujahedin would refuse to speak to a female interpreter may be an indication of a certain religious attitude, but would you agree with me that it is not a characteristic which can allow you to draw conclusions on command and control?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It would only allow us to -- to draw a conclusion on that specific incident at that particular moment in time with that individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You mentioned in response to a question from my colleague that the Mujahedin would be seen in places where fighting then took place and that this is the reason why you gained this conclusion that they were a combat indicator. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was -- normally we would find out obviously after the event about the fighting because I'd be involved in either prisoner exchange or dead-body collection and Mujahedin were always -- they always appeared as a separate entry with regard to prisoner release or dead-body exchange. It would be 25 HVO, 30 ABiH, 5 of which are Mujahedin. It was always a -- you know, a reference to it which allowed tracking, if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, we'll come to the exchange situation a little later, but for now the -- would you agree with me that on the basis of what you mentioned concerning the combat indicator that any one of your colleagues, liaison officers or others - it could be the company commanders - if they would spot or observe the presence of Mujahedin, they would then immediately report it, at least to Captain Harrison, the intelligence officer, so that this information could be included in the military infosum, because it would signal that there was an attack in the planning?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree that -- that certainly their presence of their location would be reported on return to -- to the base. But whether on its own it could indicate an attack is not -- is not true. I'd say that other assets had to be identified. It -- I would say it's this pattern. One -- one vehicle can't therefore, you know, determine a convoy. It needed to be a number of assets to be identified to try and create a picture as to what was happening. But certainly it would focus our attention, was that an area which we needed to gather more sightings to try and identify if that was going to be a -- an area where combat was going to take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And am I right, Major Bower, in saying that you personally never reported to Captain Harrison that an attack was forthcoming because you had encountered Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In fact, looking at the milinfosums, which you consulted on a daily basis, there were never such observations in the milinfosums; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I honestly can't recall. It's been some years since I've read any of the milinfosums.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, the milinfosums themselves, am I right in saying that they were not communicated to the warring factions?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I'm aware, they weren't. They were a briefing tool. I -- I don't recall any security classification on them. I mean, they were certainly used to -- to brief aid agencies. Whether hard copies were handed out, I -- I honestly don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But they were not meant to be given to the warring factions.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I -- I honestly can't recall. I mean, Simon Harrison T information officer, would be able to answer that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, these milinfosums, Major Bower, were sent upwards -- the chain of command to the United Nations' Central Bosnia command in Kiseljak, if I recall, with the purpose of informing other units in your area of what was happening in your own sector; is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's -- that's right. Because the aid agencies wanted to know which routes could be used but also each independent battalion within the UNPROFOR area needed to bring its own resupply convoys up from Split and they wanted to know, you know, was it safe or was it not. The last thing they wanted to do was drive up through Gornji Vakuf when, for example, Gornji Vakuf was suffering some very, very heavy fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, due to the nature of your work, Major Bower, and the fact that you travelled a lot in your area, did you yourself read the daily sitreps, or situation reports, which were produced by the Central Bosnia command in Kiseljak and which contained information on the other parts of Central Bosnia, for example, as to what the Canadians were doing in Visoko or what the French were doing in Kakanj?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I -- I never read any of those when I was in my general liaison officer duties. There would be an overall summary given at the 1800 hours as a general overview of what was happening either side of us. But I only read them, from what I can recall, the two weeks I was standing in as the operation officer in the ops room.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And so the same would apply, then, to the weekly military information summaries, also produced by the Central Bosnia command in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Moving on to another topic which you briefly touched upon yesterday and today. I'd like to ask you a few questions about the exchange of prisoners or dead bodies. My first question - I think I will follow your lead - the first question deals with the -- whether you were aware because you arrived in theatre at the end of April, whether the commander of an HVO brigade had been kidnapped in Zenica by foreign elements. I'm talking about the -- the name of the gentleman was Totic.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name is familiar, but I -- I can't recall specifics, I'm afraid. But the name is familiar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Were you aware that a request was presented by foreign fighters to ECMM - ECMM being the European Community Monitoring Mission - and a request was presented for the release of these foreign persons in exchange for members of the HVO? Were you aware of this fact?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I'm afraid I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Then I'll move on more quickly, then, because I had a series of questions on this incident. But did you know that the exchange itself did take place in Zenica on the 17th of May?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may well have done. At -- at that particular time in May, I was still building relations with the Red Cross and ECMM. We'd only been active for less than a month, so we hadn't really gained the confidence of the people who had already built up the relations. I don't think they wanted the new boy in there who could potentially make mistakes. So we didn't really get involved until much later, I think sort of later in May, early June, with the body and prisoner exchange. So I'm afraid I can't recall any details on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, operational control of your unit was transferred, if I recall correctly, on the 11th of May.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be about right. That would be about a week, ten days after our -- our initial arrival of our main body, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, in one of the milinfosums about this Totic incident, it was reported that the 3rd Corps had denied any link or involvement whatsoever with this exchange, but at the request of the head of ECMM in Zenica they had accepted to provide security for this exchange. Were you aware of this fact?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I'm afraid I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So I guess you are not aware either that your battalion was involved in the exchange, in the transport of the people involved.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can recall that we were continually asked to provide transport or security for various exchanges, convoys, or whatever. But specifics, I'm afraid, right at the beginning of the tour, I'm afraid everything was a bit of a blur.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And this specific event, even though it -- it concerned Mujahedin, is not something which drew your attention.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't stand out in my recollection, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the fact that it was extensively reported in milinfosums, because you're telling us today that you're not aware, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You wouldn't be surprised that it would be reported in the milinfosums.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I repeatedly noticed that my learned friend from the Defence side is making reference to milinfosums, to the contents of milinfosums he doesn't produce. It's not possible for the Prosecution and it's also not possible for the Trial Chamber to verify whether the portions of the milinfosums my learned friend is making reference to do actually form part of such milinfosums. I would therefore request that whenever my learned friend is making reference to a milinfosum and he asks questions to the witness, he should show the milinfosum to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Bourgon, you did refer to some milinfosums, in particular to General Totic. We don't know what the number of this document is. Perhaps if you had had the document you could have shown it to the witness. But the Prosecution's comment is relevant. You are referring to documents that the Trial Chamber can't assess. We don't have it, nor does the Prosecution, nor does the witness. But please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I just wanted to tell the Trial Chamber that it is the Defence's choice, since we are speaking about milinfosums in general and not particular ones, we don't want to go into all the details. It's a matter of probative value. When I ask the witness a question without showing him the document, this could reduce the weight that you might give to the information. But we don't think that this is to the detriment of the defence of the accused, because we are talking about general issues, about the type of information contained in the milinfosums.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please carry on. Yesterday you said that you would complete your cross-examination at half past 10.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] Major Bower, sorry, I lost the place I was on my page. But now you would agree with me that if you would receive a request when you were in Bosnia by 3rd Corps to exchange a Mujahedin or to recuperate the body of a Mujahedin, this was an issue that was important enough that it would be reported in the milinfosum. Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether it was reported in the military information summaries, I -- after 11 years I really can't -- can't say. But -- but I know that from notes, diaries which I've got which we -- we looked at -- it was more of a much later part of the tour it became an issue. From what I can recall, to me. How other liaison officers viewed it, I -- I can't comment for them. But certainly I took much greater note later in the tour, when from about September-time the ABiH gone to be in ascendancy, rather than in a defensive posture. And that's -- that's when I sort of made more note of it, if you like. What happened before that -- I can't recall being involved in either dead-body or prisoner exchanges which included Mujahedin earlier in the tour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, Major Bower, I -- I don't doubt the fact that you did obtain requests concerning an exchange of a prisoner or the return of a Mujahedin body. What I suggest to you, however, is that you never received and you're not able to give us a specific incident today when 3rd Corps requested an exchange of a Mujahedin or the return of a Mujahedin body specifically. Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I can recall later in the tour that we were involved in a dead-body exchange, about 50 or 60 dead bodies, with an exchange of casualties from Stari Vitez and Nova Bila. And there was a request to release Mujahedin - I can't recall whether he was a prisoner or whether he was a dead body - and the exchange was for HVO to be released in exchange for this and that we had to get the military liaison officer to talk to -- I can't remember whether it was Beba Salko or Beba in Travnik to -- as part of the link to get this whole deal going. It was a very complicated process, and this was the linkage which I referred to earlier. But whether we physically had to go to 3 Corps headquarters, I honestly can't recall whether -- I wasn't the 3 Corps liaison officer. We had somebody specifically there to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, such a request, may I suggest to you, Major Bower, that it was addressed to BritBat directly by Mujahedin themselves. Would that refresh your memory?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether it was direct by Mujahedin to us, again -- I mean, I normally got my information either from the ICRC with regard to prisoner exchange. Dead body exchange would come through the civilian hospitals because that's -- as soon as we arrived there, we'd be seen by the civilian population themselves, who would, you know, be passing on -- or pressurising us to do something. But ultimately, I would say that it's the -- the military liaison officers would -- would get any formal requests from any military headquarters on either side. I was very much -- I would get it from the aid agencies or the civilian hospitals or the civilians around those hospitals who I dealt with. I -- I can't honestly recall where those requests would -- would come from, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, Major Bower, you mentioned the name of an individual named Beba Salko. You are aware that Mr. Salko was -- had a role to play in the exchange of prisoners and that he is the one who dealt with the ICRC and other humanitarian organisations for this purpose; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I can recall, whenever I met him or I heard his name, it was -- it was either from the liaison officer from Travnik or from the Red Cross, so yes, that would -- that would be fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I would like now to move, Major Bower, to the incident of the 13 June, when you were in Guca Gora with Major Payne. Now, in this specific instance I am able to suggest to you the date of 13 June on the basis of a milinfosum.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I would ask that the witness be given the Exhibit DH71.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Major Bower, if you can just look at the first page, paragraph 1, Alpha to Golf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, assuming that my learned friend from the Defence side will ask this witness questions in relation to this milinfosum number 45, dated the 13th of June, 1993, the witness has said yesterday and he has confirmed today that he can't recall the exact date as to when he was in the area of Guca Gora. My learned colleague is suggesting to the witness that that day was the 13th of June. However, the witness is not in a position and he has confirmed it at least twice that he was in that area on that day. Therefore, the Prosecution considers any questions relating to this milinfosum very problematic, and the Prosecution objects to any questions asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the purpose of cross-examination when showing a document to the witness is just to refresh the witness's memory. The witness can say that he can't remember the date or that it's possible that the date is the right one. The purpose of cross-examination is to suggest certain information to a witness by having recourse to documents or leading questions, and the witness can confirm a document perhaps. This is just -- this is the objective of the cross-examination. I don't understand this comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. At the request of the parties, we said that it was possible in order to refresh a memory's -- a witness's memory. It was possible to show the witness a document. And this is the purpose for which you want to show the witness a document. Ask the witness your question, since the witness has had time to have a look at the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have five or six questions that relate to this document. I have another 15 minutes for the witness, and then I will have completed my cross-examination. Would you like to have the break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We'll have the break now and then you can continue for 15 minutes. So we will adjourn now and resume at five to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before giving the floor to Mr. Bourgon, regarding the objection of the Prosecution, we told the Defence that they could put the question to the witness. The problem was the following: The witness could not remember the date exactly, and that is why the Prosecution -- or rather, the Defence wanted to show him a document, to remind him -- yes, the Defence, to jog his memory. And this document, which came from his battalion, could be identified by the witness but that document needs to be interpreted in relation to other testimony that we have heard, and other persons have already been able to authenticate that document by the date of the 13th of June. As he was not the only one on the spot, this might remind the witness. And that is why it was useful to put this question to the witness. Mr. Bourgon, you have the floor to ask him your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] Major Bower, a document was shown to you shortly before the break. The only question I have based on this document - because what I'm interested in is your recollection of the events and not what is in this document - is simply that from your reading of this document, would that document arise from your trip to Guca Gora with Major Payne?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly the -- the events which are listed in the paragraph 1, they -- they look as if they refer to -- to that -- to that event, yes. It's certainly everything which is in there less the last paragraph -- subparagraph F, everything in there does correspond with -- with the events on that day. But I'm afraid the date ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: No problem with that, Major Bower. Thank you very much for this response. I'd simply like to go over the events as you recall them when you travelled with Major Payne to Guca Gora. Can you please confirm that the initial request was received from a gentleman called Thomas Osario?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's -- from what I can recall, that was his name. And we'd had dealings with him a number of times before. Mainly because he wasn't continually at our location, he'd arrive, deal with something, and then leave. So there was a novelty to -- to him being there. But he instigated it, rather than it came from -- from what I can recall, any military or aid agency chain. It came from the UN chain.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Osario spoke to you because you were the G-5. He showed you a map he had obtained from a refugee, which would indicate some kind of a mass grave. And he basically requested if you would go and take a look at this area. Is that how things happened?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's -- that's pretty much it. It was -- there wasn't too much detail. It was very much a can you go and find out what's in that area to assist? He -- he didn't want to or couldn't or was unable to -- to follow it up and therefore requested us to do it, and specifically it came to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, this was, Major Bower, some kind of new issue because you had not expected to be involved in war crimes related issue. If I am correct, you had no prior experience in this field, but you nevertheless decided, you and Major Payne, to take two Warriors up there, Warriors because you thought that soft-skin vehicles would not be appropriate. And you went to Guca Gora, and it was the second time you went to the Guca Gora area. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I can't recall if it was the second time I was in Guca Gora. It was certainly the second time I'd been up there for a specific mission, rather than my general driving around. But certainly it was the second time I was up there in an armoured vehicle. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
