utterances.text: And that would be because the first time was related, as you mentioned before, to the evacuation of the Croats which were in the monastery.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, when you arrived in Guca Gora, you were stopped by Mujahedin. And you mentioned yesterday that there were 12 to a dozen of them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, from -- from what I could recall or from what I could see, because I was in the back of the vehicle and we had to wait until we were stopped. And it was apparent that we were going to now get out and start the negotiation process, which then allowed me to -- to get out of the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when you saw the Mujahedin, you described yesterday that they had weapons. In fact, they had a heavy weapon and RPGs, and that you described also the way they were dressed. And you mentioned yesterday that their faces were covered. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Certainly some had their faces covered; not all. The individual who did most of the liaising with us, the talking, the negotiating with us, he didn't. But I would say that a -- the majority of them around the church itself had their faces covered.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the gentleman who did most of the talking with you is the one you recognised as coming from your area, who spoke the same kind of accent as your soldiers do; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The -- the Mujahedin who did the negotiating with us wasn't the British Mujahedin. The one who did the negotiating was very much Middle Eastern extraction. But we noticed, because we heard a British voice, which we obviously latched onto and tried to get that individual to -- to be more forthcoming, because we recognised his regional dialect, coming from where we recruit our soldiers. But he was very reticent to get involved in any discussion with us. So it reverted back to the Mujahedin who was from the Middle East.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So the Mujahedin you spoke to was definitely, in your opinion, someone who came -- who was a foreigner?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And he did not have his face covered.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And he is -- is he the one who refused to speak to your female interpreter?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Initially, yes, until we had this standoff. Basically two groups of people looking at each other and then us trying to speak to them and they refusing. So we were sort of just thinking what we could do. And then there was the accidental discharge of the -- of the weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: When we met earlier this week, Major Bower, you mentioned that you did not recall the presence of any media reporters there on that occasion. Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I -- I honestly can't -- excuse me. I can't recall if there were any media there, but I know that the media were very interested in -- we had a phrase "ambulance chasing." And they saw armoured vehicles, then they would invariably follow because there would be something of interest to report on. I can't recall if they followed us or if they were in the second Warrior armoured fighting vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, Major Bower, if I described a "standoff" in the following way that, it really began with the accidental discharge coming either from the Mujahedin that came from your area or some other, that luckily the bullet went over your head, that no one was hurt, but nevertheless that the traps of your vehicle were opened and immediately the crews adopted a ready position, they loaded the guns, and the Mujahedin also reacted by taking their RPG, and that for a second or a minute or part of some time the situation was indeed very tense and it was a standoff? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's -- that's a fair summary. It was -- it was a moment which concentrated the mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if I recall from our conversation, you mentioned that the fact that the position of your two Warriors, which were lower than the church, from a military point of view this was placing you into a very difficult position if you had had to react to an engagement?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, we certainly were not in an ideal position, because the -- the heavy weapon which the Mujahedin had -- because they stood on higher ground to us, which was the level of the main hull of the vehicle. They were actually looking down on our vehicles. So it was not an ideal position to be in, and I think that's what made it more tense.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, luckily enough nothing happened and the situation cooled down due to the intervention of someone who was there, but we can't really know who exactly, but the situation did calm down. And that's at that point that Major Payne entered into negotiations in order to get on this vehicle and to visit the village; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Negotiations then continued to -- to bargain, I think, to allow us to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And at that point, Mr. Thomas Osario was not there, but you had a civilian with you called Randy Rhodes, who was basically the civil affairs advisor or officer to Lieutenant Colonel Duncan; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Mr. Randy Rhodes was in the back of the Warrior with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, at that point on, you -- the deal was that you went on this Toyota pick-up truck with three or four Mujahedin, you left the troops behind, Major Payne gave orders to the troops that if he was not back after one hour that they were to force their way and find you. Nevertheless, you had no radio communications between yourself and your crew that was left behind. You had no weapons with you, or at least you were asked to leave your rifles behind, but you had your pistols with you under your flak jacket or your rain jacket, because it was raining. Is that a fair representation of the events?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, you at that point had this map which had been given to you, or this sketch, but you did not have a military map. And you recall that Major Payne, just before leaving, because he was -- he knew this was an important event and he was -- the way he felt about this event. He gave his ring to his second-in-command telling him, "If something happens to me, give it to my girlfriend," or as or as we discussed, maybe to someone else. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall him giving something to his 2IC.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And as you drove on that pick-up truck, you recall Randy Rhodes being quite upset and saying that you were taking unnecessary risks; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that -- that Randy thought it was going beyond what -- what he thought we should be doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you realise today, looking back at these events, that what was done, what was decided by -- under the command of Major Payne, to leave the troops behind, to go with unknown personnel with whom he was involved in a standoff minutes before, without weapons, without radio communications, issuing strict orders to force their way after one hour, and not having a map and not knowing exactly where you were taken is not the best way for professional military officers to conduct business. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree that it's not a way for professional military officers to conduct business. We were trying to get the job done. I would say that there was an element of military naivety in -- in this particular element. But we -- I think the British Army continues -- has always tried to work around issues and work within initiative given to us by higher authority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, my learned friend from the Defence is asking questions which make the witness judge on the professionality of his former colleagues. The Prosecution can't see the relevance of such questions and the respective answers to such questions to the issues which have to be determined in the course of this trial. The Prosecution objects against such questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The purpose behind the questions put to the witness is to get his appreciation of how he viewed the situation he was in, and this might affect the remarks that he made at the time. But I've finished with this line of questioning, and I have no intention of judging the work of this witness. It is simply to get an understanding of what he himself felt at the time. Therefore, the objection has been regulated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you will have no further questions in that direction. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] When you reached the location where you were supposed to go, on that occasion you did not find anything but you saw some smoke coming from a village called Bandol and you made your way back to this village called Bandol; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would say after about 40 minutes, 45 minutes of fruitless search, trying to relate the sketch map to an area on the ground which proved virtually impossible, we decided to call it a day. But because we'd already noticed there was a village which smoke was coming out of but we didn't realise it was Bandol until we actually got there, we decided that we would try and make better use of our -- our time, so we extracted from the area, returned back to the Warriors, and then proceeded to the village, which we then found was -- was Bandol.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And Major Bower, before we take a look at what you saw in Bandol, I'd just like to come back on the issue of what you call a military naivety of how this operation was conducted, not that the operation itself, but you mentioned something to me this week that the British Battalion, of which you were a member, really understood the true nature of the context in which you were when the issue of the Convoy of Joy happened. Is that correct? And can you explain to the Trial Chamber what is the Convoy of Joy.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- the military naivety, I think, is we were trying to put some kind of military logic. And our perception over a -- a situation which we -- we found incomprehensible, certainly from my perspective. I -- I just couldn't understand the situation of how it could be created that people would -- you know, currency became dead bodies. The bartering to get casualties back to hospitals, although there'd be women and children, could take precedence over anything else. It didn't appear to be that kind of environment. So I think we were in this period trying to understand the environment in which we were trying to operate; because up until that point the operations the battalion had been in, we were a key player. Whereas, in this situation, we weren't. We had very strict guidelines with which to adhere to and a mandate with which to operate within. So I think that's what created that -- the military naivety. The episode of the Convoy of Joy I think culminated the -- the feeling of frustration which the battalion felt because an aid convoy on nothing more than humanitarian ideals wanted to make its way to Tuzla but because of one particular ethnic mix of that convoy it was unwelcome travelling through the Lasva Valley. But because it was not operating within the United Nations mandate, we were not charged with protecting it. And so even despite repeated protests that it should come through by the UN, by the British Battalion, that it was not safe, we could not guarantee their safety, it proceeded through the Lasva Valley, was subsequently attacked, hijacked, a number of the drivers were -- were killed. A number of them were beaten. A lot of the -- the aid was stolen. And all this was done in the view of us because our mandate did not allow us to -- to get involved. And I think that was the final culmination in the feeling of frustration which forced us to re-evaluate how we did business. And on that day, we got actively engaged with combatants and killed combatants in self-protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Major Bower. I know that these incidents probably remind you of not-too-nice events. Could you confirm for the Trial Chamber that the combatants that you were engaged in and this issue of the Convoy of Joy, those people responsible for these events were the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. It was the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, moving on quickly, Major Bower, because I promised I would finish within a certain number of time. When you reached Bandol that day, you -- am I correct in saying that what you noticed was total destruction and almost every house had been burnt to the ground and that it was devastation? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's an accurate description. We certainly termed it a -- a cleansing, because the -- the roofs had disappeared off the majority of the houses. There was little ability to move into any of the houses to then rehabitate those houses. It had pretty much been destroyed, ransacked, if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, in terms of -- if we look at the result of what you saw in Bandol, in your professional experience this could not arise from battle damage; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that -- I mean, I can't say every single house was as a result of deliberate destruction. Some may have been from battle damage, of incendiary devices, whatever. But I would say that it was just too -- too complete to be -- to be as a result of purely battle damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, Major Bower, when you had the occasion early in your tour to visit the village of Ahmici, in that particular village there were houses still standing but you nevertheless came to the conclusion that this was not battle damage. Can you explain to the Trial Chamber why?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In -- in Ahmici, there were certainly some houses to the west of the -- of the road which were still habitated by -- by locals. And yet on the other side of the road, there would be complete destruction. It seemed to be selective, rather than complete clearing or destruction of houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Major Bower, one last question with respect to Guca Gora is that when you travelled through Guca Gora around -- in June - I don't want to get into a debate for the exact date - but you saw nothing in that village and in the surrounding Croat village that came even close to what you had seen in Bandol and Ahmici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, that -- from what I could see, in my entry into Guca Gora and my exit - I was in the back of the Warrior - so I didn't have much use. But certainly on the travel from Guca Gora in the Mujahedin in the Toyota pick-up, I would say that -- I believe it was Maljine we went to. It was not as -- devastating. I wouldn't say that every house had been ransacked or that, you know, the roofs had fallen in or there was systematic burning of -- of the houses. It certainly didn't compare to what was found in Bandol.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Major Bower. I have now a few questions related to the military situation as you perceived it when you were on the ground. And the military situation of the 3rd Corps itself. Were you aware that the 3rd Corps military situation was that it was -- it had to man front line with the Serbs of more than 100 kilometres?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I honestly can't recall that -- you know, the distance or who was manning what, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Would you remember, Major Bower, that there was many kilometres of front line between the ABiH and the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I can recall that -- the map itself. I mean, it was a large area of front line between them, HVO and BSA. So yes, I mean, it was a long front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And can you confirm, Major Bower, that in addition to this conflict -- or initially in this conflict - sorry - the HVO and the ABiH had been fighting together against the Serbs? Are you aware of this fact?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly I recall that the briefings we had just before we arrived that there was a -- it was a two-way conflict and either just before or as we arrived in the beginning of 1993 it, for some reason, turned into a three-way conflict. But I can't recall the reasons why or -- or when.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would you agree with me, Major Bower, that the opening of a second front for the 3rd Corps, meaning having to fight the Serbs but also the HVO, in its own area of responsibility was a very difficult military situation?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly it would not be ideal and it would stretch whatever capacity that they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would you agree, Major Bower, from your observations that the HVO used the blocking of roads and the stopping of resupply as an effective weapon against the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure about how it could be against the 3rd Corps. I know that aid convoys were -- were prevented from travelling through checkpoints, which would affect the civilian population. But how convoys could affect 3rd Corps, I'm not sure. I'm unsure of their military supply routes and how HVO could affect that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if it was convoys addressed towards the civilian population that were stopped, would that have an impact on the commander of the 3rd Corps because he would have to then probably use more resources to get those convoys through to ensure that the local population could eat? Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I'm unsure as to how 3rd Corps fitted in with the resupply -- the civilian assistance. I just saw that the impact to the humanitarian effort and how the impact of closing roads would deny aid, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'll move on more quickly to a few issues that I'm sure you will be able to confirm that. As far as Zenica is confirmed -- is concerned, sorry, there was a very important lack of food and medical supplies. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Briefly, please. You have five minutes. You've already overstepped your time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry; could you repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Would you agree that there was in Zenica a lack of medical supplies and a lack of food?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I can only comment on the Zenica hospital, which was main hospital I went to. I would certainly say that they didn't have everything that they needed but they certainly had enough to give me to take to Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Were you aware, Major Bower, of the opening of a new front in Zepce in June when you were on the ground?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware that a campaign was -- was then started in the north.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Were you aware, Major Bower, that the -- the HVO, who up until 1993 had been manning the line against the Serbs, withdrew from this line and that caused major problems for the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, all I can remember is there was reference to 3rd Corps, 1st Corps, but I can't remember exactly who was -- was where. And it was pretty much out of my area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: One last question concerning -- are you aware that at some point during your tour the HVO and the Serbs starting to deal together against the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that this was reported into the milinfosums?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid, again, I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, Major Bower, in looking back at your tour and everything you saw when you were there and looking at your military experience, would you agree with me that the commander of the 3rd Corps was placed into a situation that was extremely difficult and that it would be almost impossible to imagine a more difficult scenario for a commander to be in, militarily speaking?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dealing with -- with a civil war I imagine is -- is incredibly difficult, especially with a humanitarian aspect which -- which was prevalent. I mean, that was my focus, was the humanitarian aspect. And the suffering was -- was widespread. I don't think anybody was exempt from the implications of the effect of humanitarian aid not getting through or just the general day-to-day requirements to -- to survive. And so, yes, I'm sure the pressures were -- were quite considerable.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Major Bower, we spoke a lot of the milinfo summaries not being given a lot to -- but can you confirm that the orders, whether it be from the HVO or the 3rd Corps, were not given or that you did not have access to all the military documentation and flow of orders from the warring factions?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I can recall, military liaison officers could -- were given some indication to future operations. But generally, I think there was -- it was generally what they could gain from discussion, rather than a formal briefing or any formal documents from warring factions as to formal intent on the warring sides. But I do know that hints were given that -- for example, we were advised not to be in a certain area at a certain time on a certain date. And when a hint like that was given, it was to allow us for the humanitarian aspect and for our safety rather than anything else. But certainly no formal orders were given.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I have only two questions: Based on all the fighting that you saw in the area, would you agree with me that it would be impossible for 3rd Corps to have had only one manoeuvre brigade?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm -- I'm afraid I honestly couldn't comment on that. I really didn't get into the military capabilities of the whole corps. I only really saw it face to face at the ground level, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And my final question, Major Bower: We -- we met this week with my colleague Mr. Dixon, representing the accused Kubura, and you -- do you remember telling us at that time that you thought that the Mujahedin were an element within 7 Brigade, that this is what -- that was your opinion but that you could not be sure of this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the opinion which I formed, based on the information which I either saw myself or gained from briefings, speaking to other liaison officers. It's the impression and the opinion which -- which I came to, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But you mentioned that you could not be sure and you did not have the information to be sure of this conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall if I was physically told formally in -- whether it be a written document or a formal briefing, this was the organisation and responsibility, but I can recall that it was the -- the opinion which was formed and I can't recall how that opinion was formed, other than it would have been from discussion and from what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Major Bower. I went over my time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to the Trial Chamber, Mr. President. This concludes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I will turn to the other Defence team now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Major Bower, I have a few questions on behalf of Mr. Amir Kubura for you. Your role when you were in Central Bosnia was a reactive one; would you agree? You arrived on the scene to deal with humanitarian issues after the military operations had occurred.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly it was a result of -- it was the resultant impact of either failure of humanitarian aid to get through or the impact of specific fighting operations which caused further humanitarian issues. So it was reactive rather than proactive.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Yes. You didn't yourself observe any military operations on the ground. You weren't involved in any combat on the front lines, were you?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, do you mean by me physically involved in combat operations?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: You weren't caught up on any operations on the front lines, were you?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean did I get shot at, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: But were you ever on the front lines observing military operations?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only time I observed operations was when the HVO attacked the hill feature behind the camp, which was where we lived. And we -- that lasted a couple of days, I think. That was the only one I physically observed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Right. You were of course very interested in where military operations were taking place, because, as you said, that could assist you to plan your humanitarian efforts -- efforts and to this end you used combat indicators to try and find out where operation were taking place; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. For two things. Really to try and assist the aid agencies to predict -- there are aid requirements that they're going to need. To try and predict any ethnic migration which is going to result as a result of that operations, but also the fact we didn't want to be in the middle of a civil war in soft-skinned vehicles, for our own protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: So you avoided being involved on the front lines where military operations might be occurring.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the aim, but there were occasion when we would just happen to be in the wrong place at the wrong time and drive down a road just as two sides started against each other and we would be in the middle of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Yes. When you mentioned the term "combat indicators," really all it means is -- it's a signal or an indication of where military operations might be occurring.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. An indication of combat, rather -- rather than combat is physically taking place at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Yes. And you mentioned that the 7th Brigade was one such indicator.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: There were other indicators as well other brigades, other factors that you had to take into account.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were a number of things we had to try and identify to -- to give us some information to try and assess future intent.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Were you aware that there were other manoeuvre units in your area, including the 314th Brigade of the 3rd Corps, the 17th Krajina Brigade, and the 303 Brigade of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall the exact numbers, but certainly I -- I recall the phrase "the Krajina Brigade." But as for the specific numbers, I'm afraid I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: But you were aware that there were other manoeuvre units.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were -- there were certainly other units, but also we would look for specific vehicles which would indicate -- or road closures or whatever. You know, it was a number of assets, a number of situations which would become a combat indicator, rather than just a -- a formed body. But as what the name of those formed units were, I'm afraid I honestly can't remember now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: So to gain an accurate picture, you would agree that it was always a combination of factors, not a single factor.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, very much so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: It's correct that you never observed the 7th Brigade involved in combat on the front lines. You mentioned earlier on that you observed the HVO in combat, but not the 7th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Did you know that the 7th Brigade was involved in military operations in Ovnak, which was in your area, at the beginning of June 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall the name of -- of that place, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: And did you know that the brigade thereafter was involved in military operations in Kakanj, which was not in your area, but did you know this after that in June 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Again, I'm afraid, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: And did you know that the brigade was involved in military operations towards the end of July in Fojnica and Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I believe afraid after 11 years I really can't recall. It's been sometime since I read a milinfosum.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Mm-hm. What about in August and September on Mount Igman, near Sarajevo? Did you know the 7th Brigade was involved in operations there?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sarajevo was so far away from -- we couldn't even get to it, so I'm afraid we had little interest in what was happening there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: But did you know anything about where they were at that time?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I honestly recall. Whether we were briefed, whether we weren't briefed, I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: What about in November in Vares?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: November I would have been looking at leaving. I think I left about the 6th or 7th of November. So I think my last thing was in Stupni Dol [phoen]. So I don't recall anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Yes. You said that the 7th Brigade headquarters, to your knowledge, was situated at the music school; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: You never went into the music school, did you?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: You never met any of the commanders of the 7th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Did you ever meet Mr. Amir Kubura?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I can't recall. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Did you know who he was at the time?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have known who he was at the time, but -- but now I'm afraid I can't recall what position he held.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Mm-hm. But you never met him when you were there.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Did you know that there was an assassination attempt on him by the foreign mercenaries that you described earlier on?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm afraid I -- I don't recall that incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: You didn't know that the headquarters of the 7th Brigade was actually at a place called Bilmiste, did you?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as I was aware, it was at the music school near -- near the ICRC.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Did you know where Bilmiste was? Does the name ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm I afraid, no. No. Right now I'm afraid I couldn't recall where it would be on a map.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: So you don't know it's about a kilometre -- just over a kilometre away from the music school.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid to say. 11 years after leaving Zenica, I'm afraid, you know, I would have trouble finding my way from UNHCR to ICRC.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: 11 years on, assessing the situation now, would you agree with me that your knowledge of the 7th Brigade at the time was fairly limited?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that when it related to what I had to do, you know, it's -- it's still quite clear. But as to -- to how it was in the overall campaign, unless it impacted on what I was trying to do, or it created work for me, I'm afraid no -- the same as any other unit. I'm afraid I can't recall the majority of names of any other units I dealt with -- dealt with there. Their bodies, their prisoners, or the resultants of their clashes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: So you didn't have detailed knowledge of the structure of the 7th Brigade, the subordination and composition of the brigade, did you?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Along with any other unit, no. I wasn't the military liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: You mentioned that you first came across foreign fighters. You called them mercenaries in your testimony - when you went up in May -- it appears the date now is June -- with Major Kent-Payne. At that time, you didn't meet any members of the 7th Brigade when you met with these mercenaries you described, did you?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall, you know, whether there was a specific identification of a brigade, other than the badges they had on their arms, the way they looked, the way they appeared, and the way they acted was an indication that they were Mujahedin, which I think is, you know, how we referred to them at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: They were all foreigners, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ones which I saw and interacted with, or tried to interact with were certainly foreign, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: You said earlier on in your testimony when you withdrew from that area you went through a -- a buffer zone and then you came across soldiers from the Bosnian Army; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The -- the we would -- when we left the area of Guca Gora with the Mujahedin in it, we then entered into this buffer area where there were ABiH, because they were then manning their checkpoints. And then we moved into the HVO area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Mm-hm. The foreigners that you met up in Guca Gora, they never mentioned anything to you about the 7th Brigade. You never discussed that issue, did you?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They weren't that talkative.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: You were only discussing getting access to the area.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We found that it was best not to try and broaden a fairly difficult time. It was to try and keep things fairly simple, very narrow band.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: You had no intelligence on these foreign fighters, did you?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had information to -- to suggest that there were a -- an element of foreign mercenaries on both sides. But information as to who they were specifically and from which regions by number was -- was very sketchy. It was purely on what people had seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: So you had no intelligence about under whose control they were, did you?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Me personally, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: There's no intelligence report, there's no document which shows under whose control they were, is there?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I can't say whether Simon Harrison, the military officer, had anything which he dealt with at a higher chain. I wasn't involved in that element of the -- of the campaign, so I'm afraid I honestly can't say whether there is or there isn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: But you haven't got anything yourself, have you?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally have got nothing, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Major Bower.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Dixon. I turn now to Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Major, I have a few questions covering four different issues. And they all are a result of the cross-examination by my learned friends from the Defence side. Major, you described your relation with the HVO in answering a question of my learned friends from the Defence side as being some sort of shuttle diplomacy. Did there come a time during your tour in Central Bosnia you would describe the difficulties you may have experienced with the ABiH 3rd Corps in using the very same term?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would. It would very much at the end of the tour and the last eight weeks or so, when the ascendancy had changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And can you please describe for the benefit of the Trial Chamber what these difficulties thereabout about which made you now describe as "shuttle diplomacy."

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Initially there would be a request. It was invariably for an evacuation of civilians who were going to die if we couldn't get them out of normally a surrounded pocket. Invariably it would be Croats out -- out of the Nova Bila hospital or it would be Muslims out of the Stari Vitez pocket. So there would need to be negotiation with -- initially with an HVO side or a BiH side, because we were going to have to cross the opposing side's front line to get permission to move civilians in my vehicle, which was something that obviously they wanted to be sure that we weren't moving combatants. So you would enter into a negotiation. And as soon as you went to the opposing side to say, for example, "I need to move three wounded people through this checkpoint. I don't want them to be captured or taken off our hands," there would invariably be, "Yes, you can but we won't." And there would then be a condition attached to the initial request, which would require me to go back to the initiator, where we're talking about people who are going to die, to say, "Yes, we're going to move them," but they now attached a position, "Do you agree?" And that would result in a toing and froing of negotiation while the wounded people are pretty much almost left out of the original request and they get lost in the negotiations. And it would result normally in -- in failure, because it became too difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Let's move on to -- to the second issue. Major, to your knowledge, is propaganda and false information of the public something that is used in wartimes by all warring factions?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would -- I would certainly agree that there is an element of misinformation which is -- which is employed by -- by all warring sides. It's -- you always want to try and gain an advantage.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And does this general statement also apply for the ABiH 3rd Corps while you were in the area of Central Bosnia in 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that there -- again, rumour was -- was rife on both sides. And to be honest, unless it was a claim which was clearly outrageous which we, you know, just didn't have the time to investigate, you know, we would ask about it, but if we couldn't verify, deny, confirm, we would just sort of leave it be. But I would say that certainly I can't recall any one side sort of being markedly different in one way or another using this -- rumour was rife.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Let's move on to the third issue out of the four I wish to address with you, Major Bower.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can the witness please be provided with Prosecution Exhibit P100 and Prosecution Exhibit P101. The first one is the milinfosum number 37, the 5th of June, 1993; and the second one is the milinfosum of 23rd June 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Major, before you actually do read the milinfosums - and I will draw your attention to certain portions - when in the course of information that formed part or when it became known to the person who provided the information that finally formed part of the milinfosum, when the source was questionable, or in situations in which the source had to be confirmed, was this made clear in the milinfosum, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I can recall, the standard practice of trying to identify a source, whether it was confirmed, unconfirmed, reliable, unreliable, or if it was from a -- a certain person who was known regularly, then their name may appear. But I can't recall if it was a -- if it was a set requirement to have information entered, that it had to be attached to a name.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: I'm not necessarily talking about certain names. If you, however, Major, could have a look, please, at the milinfosum of 5th of June, 1993, page 1, paragraph 2. There's a section at the very end which starts with "Comment." And it reads as follows: "The reliability of this information cannot be assessed." And if you would also, Major, please have a look at the other milinfosum of 23rd of June, 1993, page 3, at the top under "b" there is a section, "Comment". It's a section of fine -- of five lines, and it reads, B/C/S: "Attempted to verify this claim by visiting the areas mentioned." From what you got to know about the milinfosums, would you describe or was it typical that such information about the reliability of information was contained in milinfosums?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would certainly say that there was a desire to confirm from -- certainly something which -- if something was deemed important, it would invariably try and find, if we can, another way of identifying or confirming or -- or denying. I don't think it was possible to do it every single time, but it was certainly -- it was a benefit if you could.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Was it, Major, was it typical in order to bolster the reliability of the other information contained in the milinfosums to include such comments which actually identify areas which may be questionable?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly that's the aim. I mean, the battalion had recently before this deployment come out of West Belfast, where we were very much in the an intelligence-gathering role, and so it was standard practice for us to try and lend some credence to commanders who were going to have to make a decision as to the reliability of -- or the strength of the information contained in the summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can the two milinfosums please be removed from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Major, there's -- there is the fourth and the last issue I wanted to address with you in re-examination, and that concerns the exchange of prisoners and dead bodies. You said yesterday during the examination-in-chief - and you confirmed it today during the cross-examination - that Mujahedin were exchanged together with other ABiH soldiers and that the regular phrase used in such exchange --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't think that the witness confirmed what the Prosecution has just mentioned, allegedly that Mujahedins were exchanged for -- with soldiers from the BH Army. He certainly mentioned exchanges. He should elaborate on that. But he never confirmed that soldiers had been exchanged at the same time. He said the contrary, in fact. He said that they were always separate issues, as far as the Mujahedin are concerned. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Withopf, have you taken note of these comments? Your question suggests that there were exchanges that concerned soldiers and Mujahedin. According to the transcript and according to what the witness said, the witness did mention exchanges but he wasn't that precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I am very well prepared to rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Major, whilst you were or at occasions you were involved in the exchange of prisoners and dead bodies, were there occasions in which Mujahedin were exchanged for HVO soldiers together with other ABiH soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the latter part of the tour, yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: How were such exchanges organised? Can you please provide the Chamber with some detail in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information would -- would come to me normally from the Red Cross, and they would require protection, so the military liaison officers would negotiate local cease-fires, and a containment area would be set up by the battalion cordoning off an area normally between the front lines, providing the protection. We would arrange for the bodies to be collected. And if it meant digging them up, that's what we did. The prisoners would be -- normally that would be done by the Red Cross, but they would pretty much be brought into a centre. And then verification would have to take place until both sides were happy, and then we would collapse the cordon and everyone would go away.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The witness's answer is something that we heard yesterday. We heard about the organisation of the exchanges. We heard about the information obtained. We heard about the bodies on the ground. We've heard all of this information. We heard this information yesterday. I don't know what the question is that the Prosecution wants to ask. Maybe it's the same one that I wanted to ask: Were there any requests for prisoners or for the bodies of Mujahedin, were there any requests made by the BH Army? And I think that's the question that should be asked and I think that the witness has already answered this question. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, my learned colleague from the Defence had sufficient time to answer his questions [sic] during the cross-examination, and he should please leave it to the Prosecution to ask further questions which are a result of questions my learned colleague asked during the cross-examination. The issue of the exchange of prisoners, that's correct, that has been discussed yesterday in examination-in-chief. The issue has been revisited by my learned friend from the Defence today. And resulting from the answers the witness has given in answering questions during cross-examination, the Prosecution wishes to ask the witness follow-up questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So ask your follow-up questions, because the Trial Chamber was in any event going to ask this witness about this matter. So it would be best to have this done immediately. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Major, you were just - for the benefit of the Trial Chamber - describing how such exchanges were organised on the ground, and it, from your answer, becomes obvious that both parties to the conflict were involved in it. Was the ABiH -- were representatives of the ABiH involved in the exchange of prisoners, including in the exchange of ABiH soldiers together with Mujahedin, to your knowledge, please?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I can recall, there -- the groupings came together, depending on which prisons they had been held in. How the military liaison officers had negotiated with the various HVO, ABiH headquarters to arrange the cease-fires and the agreement in numbers - because there was always contention - the HVO would systematically say that if they were going to release some Mujahedin, then they wanted two HVO in return, which again started further negotiations. So there was a great deal of set-up for these exchanges and invariably the exchanges would collapse because agreement couldn't be reached. From what I can recall, I can just recall total numbers and we would be informed that there were a number, if there were any Mujahedin in that group, it was a number that was set alongside the -- the ABiH. So, for example, 25 ABiH, 5 Mujahedin would be incorporated in an exchange for however many HVO the agreement was for. But as to how the negotiations for those numbers were reached, I wasn't involved in those specifically. I was very much sort of on the ground with the ICRC doing the face-to-face checking of who they were and transporting of the bodies or prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Major, to enable the exchange of prisoners on the ground and to come to cease-fire agreements for the exchange of prisoners on the ground, to your knowledge at what level was this decided in respect to both warring factions?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depending on the number and what we were trying to do, from what I can recall, local cease-fires dealing with local commanders could be arranged for casualty evacuations. But for large -- for large elements, because it normally involved gathering prisoners from further afield, rather than close to the front line, it normally resulted in having to go higher up the chains of command within HVO and ABiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And just in clarification of an answer you gave just a minute or two minutes ago. The exchange was on the one hand side HVO soldiers or dead bodies, dead HVO soldiers' bodies, and, on the other hand, ABiH soldiers and Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it -- the numbers were generally grouped together to the two opposing sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And the ABiH soldiers and the Mujahedin were considered being one of the two opposing sides.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were. But I would -- I would say that the numerical value in the Mujahedin by the -- viewed by the HVO, hence they would sometimes request a one-for-two element.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Major Bower.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, the Prosecution has no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Judges will have some questions for you. Has the Defence, following the re-examination, anything to say? No. Good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Major, this question of exchanges is absolutely not clear. What we would like to know is whether you were a witness and took part in an exchange, you yourself, not what you knew about it but your own personal involvement during the six-month period between June and November, did you take part in an operation of that kind?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was only one operation or several?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was several. No more than three or four. The Red Cross liked to do it on their own. It was invariably when the situation, the military situation, was too dangerous for them, they needed the protection of us. Generally they would try and organise it on their own. So it was very much in the latter parts of the tour when we had this multiple linkage that I would get involved. And it was generally either setting the conditions or it was assisting in transport, because the ICRC had little in its own integral vehicles to move large numbers. As the end of the tour came, it moved from one or two prisoners to numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you transported prisoners in your vehicles. These prisoners, when the HVO wanted prisoners, did they have a list with the names of prisoners or did they say, "We have 20; take 20"? Did they have a list with their names on them.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could vary. But generally it would come down to their wanting a list of names. Initially it would start with numbers. And then as the negotiations proceeded, lists of names would be required, certainly by the Red Cross. And they would get involved in that. We would tend to stand back and let their experience and expertise run with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These lists, which apparently existed, they were given to the Red Cross. But did the British Battalion have in its possession such lists, or were you simply satisfied by putting the individuals in your vehicles and transporting them from point A to point B without knowing who exactly you had in those vehicles, unless the Red Cross gave you a copy of that list? You're a military officer. My question is a very specific one. A military man would normally answer with precision this particular question. Was it carried out in an empirical manner, or was it part of a military process, which is not quite the same thing? So what could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The primary role and the prime mover in all these were the aid agencies, not the British Battalion. The Red Cross would furnish the lists. All we would be required to do was set conditions of safety and protection. We would ensure that the right people were in the right place - those are the aid agency people - and any commission people which had to be moved to the front lines to verify who the individuals were. But it was up to the aid agency, who had prime responsibility, to ascertain who was being put on those vehicles and that they are the right people who would be accepted for exchange. That was not our concern. We were there to protect and to transport and to set conditions to allow this exchange, whether it be prisoners or dead bodies, to take place. The only times we got involved with lists was during the Nova Bila evacuations from the hospitals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A final question, and then I will give the floor to the other Judges. When these persons boarded your vehicles, these vehicles belonged to the British Battalion. You said a moment ago that there were soldiers, that is, Mujahedin. On what basis are you saying that they were soldiers and what leads you to believe that among the prisoners there were no civilians? How do you make a distinction between military people and civilians?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, who got onto the vehicles was not our concern. We provided the transport, the driver and the vehicle. It was up to the Red Cross to identify the individuals, walk them to the transport, and put them on the transport. We were concerned with looking out to any threat and not looking in. It was a Red Cross, from the experiences which I had, it was a Red-Cross-run operation. We were providing the assets and setting conditions to allow it to happen. The Red Cross would have preferred not to -- not to have us there at all, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One more question, because I could go on like this for hours because the subject is so important that it would merit many questions. You told us that in your battalion there was an intelligence officer with a team under him, but this intelligence officer certainly existed. Was your intelligence officer present and did he debrief the prisoners during the exchanges?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. He had no recourse to go out there at all. It was -- again, and the Red Cross wouldn't have let us do it. It would have jeopardised further Red Cross issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Just a few questions on that, what you have said yesterday and also today on the subject of looting. Yesterday you told us something on the phenomena of looting you have seen in Guca Gora, and you also told us something about looting in general, especially the different stages of looting, if I remember correctly the whole thing. As far as Guca Gora is concerned, you were visiting the town with -- together with Kent-Payne and Randy Rhodes and you were in a vehicle on your way to Maljine. And if I recall well, you said this morning: "Apart from this incident at the roadblock we didn't leave our vehicle." So you just crossed Guca Gora; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. When we arrived in -- in Guca Gora, it was only when the vehicles stopped and it was quite clear that the interpreter in the back of the vehicle had to get out, that's when I then got out. And it was -- that's when I saw where we were. But obviously in a very localised part of -- of the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: You didn't descend from your vehicle at other parts of Guca Gora.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The only time I had seen Guca Gora was then when we drove from that checkpoint, where we were stopped, on the route in the back of the vehicle with the Mujahedin to go to Maljine. That was the only part which I saw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: And then back the same route to -- back into the vehicle, inside it, and then to leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So what you saw in Guca Gora concerning looting was exclusively based on -- on your view in this vehicle. That is right?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: You said something about looting. And if I recall it not correctly, please correct me. You saw objects on the street and there was a lot of traffic. You also said, if I recall well, furniture was taken also from the church. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. What -- what I can recall is that there were -- there was furniture outside the church.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the houses which we saw, although not in the destruction of what we saw in Bandol, but there were house objects, whether it be chairs, bedding, that kind of thing, was outside or had been thrown outside. And it was -- you know, searches, you know, the places had been searched. And that's really all I can describe. The physical looting -- I would say that we saw people carrying items. But whether it was just moving stuff around, searching, it's difficult to say because we couldn't stop and assess over a period of time. We were driving through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Did you report this to -- to Captain Harrison, the -- were you debriefed by Captain Harrison on this topic?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Vaughan Kent-Payne spoke to Captain Harrison and I spoke to him very briefly because he was going to get the same thing, and Major Vaughan Kent-Payne, obviously being in the command turret, could obviously see a lot more than I could. So I just told the result on what I had been asked to do. And to be honest, it didn't really feature on the milinfosum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So you saw people being active in looting; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw people carrying household items.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I couldn't ascertain from, you know, where --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Whether it was looting or not.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't ascertain where those items had come from and where they then were taking them too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Yes. And who were -- who were those persons? Like, civilians or other people?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again -- no, the military aspect. It was all within the Mujahedin who we saw in that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: But the person who you saw carrying objects, were they Mujahedin or civilians?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what we could tell from the distance, obviously we were still in a -- in a moving vehicle. It was all within the area where the Mujahedin were, because from Guca Gora to the village where we started looking for the -- the grave site, it was Mujahedin in both locations. So, you know, the -- the assumption was that if they're in Guca Gora and the village we were looking in and they were along the road which we travelled to, that's how we made the assumption that all those people in that area were the Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: But those people you saw carrying objects in that place, did they have military uniforms or ...?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I can recall, yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Yes. And was there any attempts to -- to stop the looting? Have you seen in the short moment you passed probably this -- this village?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I would say -- I would say it was relatively calm in the area that we were in. There didn't seem to be -- there were a lot of people walking around not necessarily concerned about potential shoots against them. So I would say that it was -- it was a generally calm atmosphere which we were in from -- from that perspective.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Nevertheless, you said yesterday there was quite a lot of traffic.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a lot of foot traffic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Foot traffic.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Did you also see lorries or things of that kind?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall, sir. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Yesterday you also talked about looting in general and the various stages of looting. If I remember well, you described three different stages of looting. I take it - but I'm not sure - that you saw this phenomenon at various times.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Not only in Guca Gora but other places.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: More often than not the whole set we saw was actually when it happened outside our camp in September/October-time. But generally we may catch the latter element of it, either families moving into -- into houses which had previously been occupied by others, you know, the moving of items being moved across streets in barrows, that sort of thing. But the only time I can say I physically saw, you know, the full spectrum of it was during the attack at Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't hear you. The attack on ...?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the -- the full spectrum of this -- of this looting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The initial, then, sort of subsequent and then actual taking houses over was during the attack at Grbavica, next to our camp, which is when the HVO attacked the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I see. So your observations were prior to HVO territory, so to speak, and to -- to the territory under the -- the domination of the Bosnian Army.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Did you see other occurrences of looting on the territory of the Bosnian Army?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: You didn't. Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon, do you wish to make any further clarifications following the answers given to the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence has no questions relating to exchange, but just a point of clarification regarding looting, which might perhaps be of assistance to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Major, can you confirm that when you were in Guca Gora the situation was calm, as you said, but the fighting was over for some time? Am I correct in saying that?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It -- it's fair to say that the -- the fighting had actually finished by that stage. It was -- there was definitely not a -- a requirement for the forces to -- to take precautions from being engaged by HVO forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And one last question, which basically it's a comment you made when we met earlier this week, and I thought that was a very good illustration. When referring to Bosnia, you said that you tried to establish a parallel. And you mentioned to me, "In the UK, people play football and smoke. And in Bosnia, people wear parts of uniforms and they have weapons." Can you explain that a bit for the benefit of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution noticed several times that my learned friend from the Defence is making reference to what has been said in previous meetings of Defence counsel with the witness. The Prosecution is aware of such meetings, and this is by no means what we object to, by no means. However, there are two issues involved: Whenever my learned friend from the Defence side reports about such meetings, he's basically testifying and he's providing hearsay evidence to the Chamber. And the second issue is the question he just asked the witness, that does not result from any -- at least, it is not obvious that it would result from any of the questions which have been asked in the course of the cross-examination, the re-examination, or in respect to questions which have been asked by the Trial Chamber. The Prosecution objects against the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With regard to the question about looting only, it is very difficult to see a link. Could you please explain what the link is between looting and the fact that Bosnians bore weapons; whereas, the British played football and smoked. It's rather difficult to see the link. Maybe we must have misunderstood.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Chamber -- the question by the Chamber was whether the people carrying personal belongings were wearing uniforms. And I was going to say that there were many people wearing uniforms in Bosnia. My learned friend says it is hearsay. I don't think so, because he is the person who observed this. The meeting -- the purpose of these meetings is to specify what he said in his statements, so I see no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can ask him the question whether the people carrying fridges and I don't know what were wearing uniforms. That question is directly linked to the other questions. So go ahead with your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Major Bower, the question was put to you whether those people were wearing uniforms, and your response to the Honourable Judge was yes. Is it right that many people in Bosnia wear uniforms, whether they are soldiers or not soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I -- I would say it's fair to say that there would be some element of people would wear a uniform or a camouflage jacket or a pair of camouflage trousers. They may not be carrying a weapon. It -- it really did depend. It comes back to -- we had the impression of the army was the people and the people was the army. It depended on what they were doing in that particular area at the time. But I'd say yes, people wore uniform or didn't wear uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The Defence has no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dixon, any more questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. No further questions for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. The Prosecution has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Bower, your testimony that took place over two days is over. You have answered questions from the Prosecution, also from the Defence during the cross-examination, as well as questions from the Judges. Thank you for coming from the United States to testify and contribute to the establishment of the truth. And, of course, we wish you a safe journey to your residence, where you are an instructor, and we wish you every success in your military career.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf, what about the planning for next week?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, there are actually three issues the Prosecution wishes to address. I don't think it will take longer than ten minutes. And one of them, of course, is the planning for next week. For that purpose, can we please go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Let's go into private session. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
